source.title: Asymptotic Risk of Overparameterized Likelihood Models: Double Descent Theory for Deep Neural Networks

page_placements.theme: Variance sources, reproducibility and post-threshold variance reduction

record.tranche_reason: The study derives asymptotic risk curves using likelihood and random-matrix theory, and also runs a width sweep on deep networks; these are different methods from the original empirical studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own asymptotic risk results and a CIFAR-10 experiment. The experiment measures test-set cross-entropy loss variance, not test error. Results cited from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper derives asymptotic risk bounds for general penalized likelihood models, including parallel deep networks, ensembles and ResNets. The bound with τ=0 has the double-descent shape in γ=p/n. The method is theoretical, not the originals' empirical sweeps. The CIFAR-10 experiment measures only the variance component of cross-entropy loss, which is a different construct from test error or risk.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also stress that parallelization (divisible, block-sparse structure) is a sufficient condition for the bound and for double descent in deep models. They note densely connected networks may not satisfy it. They present the CIFAR-10 loss-variance experiment as supporting this.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops theoretical asymptotic risk bounds for penalized likelihood models using Fisher information and random-matrix methods, with a CIFAR-10 width-sweep experiment; it does not reproduce the original study's full empirical sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The risk curve changes with the limiting regularization coefficient τ. In the CIFAR-10 experiment, both architectures begin their reported descent at width 8; the parallel network is described as more similar to double descent.

fits_no_version.finding: In CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 width sweeps (1 to 64 filters, n=25,000), the variance component of test cross-entropy loss rises and then falls, with descent starting at width 8. The rise-and-fall is more pronounced for the M=3 parallel network.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The variance term of the test loss is unimodal in network width, and parallel structure sharpens this shape.

record.problems: The theoretical result is a bound and depends on Assumptions 1–4. The empirical section reports loss variance rather than test error, uses one dataset and 10 replications, and its numerical curve values are figure-only.

untested.parts: No test-error sweep over model size in deep networks. The width sweep reports only the loss-variance component.
The theory is in the ratio γ only. There is no test of whether more samples raise error at fixed p, and no sample-size experiment.
Exact risk is not derived, only an upper bound. The peak at the interpolation threshold is not shown for actual risk. There is no empirical test-error curve across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across axes.
Label-noise dependence, multiple peaks, and removal under optimally tuned regularization are not tested.
No recounting of complexity by effective parameters.

missing.what: The singularity sits in the variance term; the bias term is bounded by λr². This bears on V6's claim that the peak is variance-driven.
The regularized bound under uniform and semi-circular spectral measures gives roughly similar curves, a robustness check of the τ>0 result across Fisher spectra.
The prediction-risk (L2) bound has the same shape as the estimation bound for nonlinear regression.

record.verdict_notes: The theoretical results are upper bounds under strong assumptions, including M ≫ p^{3/4} sub-models. The empirical part measures only the variance component of the loss with weight decay on, and does not locate an interpolation threshold, so it cannot speak to V1.

versions.untested_parts: The deep-network width sweep reports loss variance, not test error.
No sweep over training epochs or training time is reported.
No experiment varies the number of training samples near the interpolation threshold and measures test error.

The theory applies under the paper's assumptions and gives an asymptotic risk bound, not unrestricted exact risks for every model class. The deep-network experiment does not locate an interpolation threshold.
The study does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
The study does not test whether label noise causes the peak, whether peaks split into multiple peaks, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
The study does not re-count complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether this turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: penalized maximum likelihood estimator for general likelihood models
rows.operation_detail: Derives the asymptotic variance risk bound as the parameter-to-sample ratio γ varies with τ = 0.
rows.measure: asymptotic variance risk bound, expressed by the extended Stieltjes transform
rows.value: For γ < 1, lim hγ,0(a) = γ/(1−γ); for γ > 1, lim hγ,0(a) = 1/(γ−1). The paper identifies this as the double-descent curve.
rows.note: The curve diverges at γ = 1 and decreases for γ > 1. This is an asymptotic risk bound, not an empirical measurement of exact risk.
rows.check: This is an upper bound on the variance term, not the risk. A diverging bound at γ=1 does not show the actual risk peaks there. The bound does stay finite and decreasing for γ>1. The full risk bound adds a non-vanishing bias term λr², so it is not a full double-descent curve. 'Observed' overstates the result.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine. The transform equals γ/(1−γ) for γ<1 and 1/(γ−1) for γ>1. It enters an upper bound on the variance term with multiplicative constants; the estimation-risk bound additionally contains a bias bound. These bounds do not establish the shape of actual risk.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2, Theorems 2–3; Section 3.2.1, Proposition 1 and Corollary 2.
source_check.problem: A bound with an interpolation singularity cannot establish even a partial occurrence of the actual-risk curve required by V4.

rows.subject: penalized maximum likelihood estimator for general likelihood models
rows.operation_detail: Compares asymptotic risk curves under zero and positive limiting regularization.
rows.value: For τ > 0, the paper reports a different regularized asymptotic risk curve, analogous to the ridge-regression risk curve.
rows.note: The paper reports dependence on regularization but does not establish that optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
rows.check: With τ>0 the bound (Example 1, Dirac spectrum) is finite at γ=1, a ridge-like curve. This shows regularization removes the divergence in the bound, which bears on V6. It does not show the peak is gone under optimal tuning. Figure 2 uses only τ=γ.

relationships.condition: General likelihood models satisfying Assumptions 1–4 (e.g. parallel DNNs with many sub-networks, ensembles, ResNet via minimax), τ=0
relationships.reason: The variance-risk bound diverges at γ=1 and decreases for γ>1, matching the linear-regression double-descent curve for nonlinear models (R1). It is an upper bound only.
relationships.display_finding: The variance-risk upper bound diverged at γ=1 and decreased for γ>1, establishing this shape for the bound rather than actual risk.
